content: Ascorbic acid injection is a form of vitamin C that is approved by the FDA for the treatment of scurvy. It is particularly useful in cases of acute vitamin C deficiency or when oral absorption is uncertain. Common side effects include reactions at the injection site, such as pain and swelling, diarrhea, iron overload, and kidney stone formation. For adults, ascorbic acid is typically administered orally. However, in cases where oral administration is not feasible or malabsorption is suspected, it can be given intramuscularly, intravenously, or subcutaneously. Intramuscular administration is the preferred parenteral route due to better utilization of the vitamin. When administered intravenously, it is recommended to dilute the solution in a large volume of normal saline or glucose to reduce adverse reactions. The average daily dose for prevention is 70 to 150 mg, while doses of 300 mg to 1 gram daily are recommended for treating scurvy. In severe cases, up to 6 grams have been administered without evidence of toxicity. For wound healing, 300 to 500 mg daily for 7 to 10 days is generally sufficient, while severe burns may require 1 to 2 grams daily. In other conditions requiring increased vitamin C, doses three to five times the daily recommended allowance are often adequate. Aseptic techniques should be used, and any remaining solution should be discarded within 4 hours of opening the vial. The solution should be inspected for clarity and the absence of particulate matter before administration. There are no contraindications for ascorbic acid injection. However, excessive doses over extended periods should be avoided in diabetics, patients prone to recurrent kidney stones, those undergoing stool occult blood tests, and individuals on sodium-restricted diets or anticoagulant therapy. Mild soreness at the injection site may occur, and rapid intravenous administration can cause temporary faintness or dizziness. During pregnancy, ascorbic acid injection should only be used if clearly necessary, as its effects on fetal development are not well studied. Caution is also advised when administering the drug to nursing mothers. There is limited guidance on its use in pediatric, geriatric, or immunocompromised patients, as well as in those with renal or hepatic impairment. Ascorbic acid is a water-soluble vitamin essential for collagen formation, tissue repair, and various metabolic processes, including tyrosine metabolism, folic acid conversion, carbohydrate metabolism, and iron absorption. It also plays a role in resistance to infections and cellular respiration. Deficiency leads to scurvy, which primarily affects collagenous structures, bones, and blood vessels. Administration of ascorbic acid reverses these symptoms. The injection is a clear, colorless to slightly yellow sterile solution containing 500 mg of ascorbic acid per milliliter, along with disodium edetate, sodium hydroxide, and water for injection. It is free of preservatives and should be stored between 2° to 8°C (36° to 46°F) and protected from light. Ascorbic acid injection is available in 50 mL sterile dispensing vials. It is marketed under the brand name ASCORBIC ACID® and should be stored in its carton until use.
